title: Content negotiation and formatters (JSON, XML, custom)
hook: Content negotiation decides whether your API responds with JSON, XML, or another format based on the Accept header and your registered output formatters. Most modern Web APIs fix JSON only — but interviews still test how formatters plug into ObjectResult execution.

blocks.text: When a handler returns an object or Ok(dto), ASP.NET Core wraps it in ObjectResult and selects an IOutputFormatter based on content negotiation. The client sends Accept: application/json (or */*), and the framework picks System.Text.JsonOutputFormatter by default. If the client requests an unsupported type, the API may return 406 Not Acceptable — unless you configure a default formatter regardless of Accept. Input formatters (IInputFormatter) deserialize request bodies on the way in; output formatters serialize on the way out.

entries.plainDefinition: Selecting a response representation based on Accept, Accept-Charset, and registered formatters.
IOutputFormatter implementation that writes a CLR object to the response stream with a specific content type.
IInputFormatter reads the request body into a model — paired with [Consumes] attribute.
Declares response content types for an action — affects negotiation and OpenAPI.

blocks.text: Most greenfield Web APIs standardize on JSON and disable XML negotiation — simpler clients, smaller payloads, better tooling. You still need to understand negotiation when integrating with legacy SOAP/XML consumers, returning CSV exports, or debugging why a client gets 406. Misconfigured formatters cause empty bodies, wrong Content-Type headers, or camelCase vs PascalCase mismatches.

blocks.title: JSON-only is the modern default
blocks.body: Configure AddControllers().AddJsonOptions() once. For public REST APIs, document JSON only in OpenAPI and return 415/406 honestly when clients send wrong Content-Type or Accept. Do not register XML unless a consumer requires it.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Handler returns ObjectResult
items.body: Ok(dto), return dto, or Results.Ok(dto) all become ObjectResult with the value.

items.title: Read Accept header
items.body: ObjectResultExecutor asks OutputFormatterSelector to rank formatters against Accept values.

items.title: Match formatter
items.body: First IOutputFormatter that CanWriteResult returns true wins — typically JSON.

items.title: Set Content-Type
items.body: Response header set to application/json; charset=utf-8.

items.title: Serialize value
items.body: Formatter writes async to Response.Body using configured JsonSerializerOptions.

diagram.title: Content negotiation flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Handler returns OrderDto] --> B[ObjectResult]
  B --> C{Accept header}
  C -->|application/json| D[SystemTextJsonOutputFormatter]
  C -->|application/xml| E{XmlFormatter\nregistered?}
  E -->|yes| F[Xml output]
  E -->|no| G[406 Not Acceptable\nor default JSON]
  D --> H[Response body JSON]

snippet.label: Configure JSON as the primary formatter
snippet.explanation: JsonOptions apply to controller output formatters. HttpJsonOptions apply to minimal API Results.Json and WriteAsJsonAsync. Keep both aligned to avoid inconsistent serialization.

snippet.label: [Produces] and fixed content type
snippet.explanation: [Produces] documents and constrains response types for OpenAPI. File() bypasses JSON formatters — sets Content-Type and Content-Disposition directly.

snippet.label: Adding XML formatter (legacy interop)
snippet.explanation: XML formatters are opt-in. Public JSON-only APIs should not add this unless required. XmlSerializer respects public properties; DataContractSerializer uses [DataContract] attributes.

snippet.label: Custom output formatter for CSV
snippet.explanation: Custom formatters implement CanWriteType and WriteResponseBodyAsync. Register in MvcOptions.OutputFormatters. Client sends Accept: text/csv to trigger it.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Mismatched JsonOptions vs HttpJsonOptions — controllers and minimal APIs serialize differently. Returning anonymous objects with circular references — serializer throws. Expecting XML without AddXmlSerializerFormatters. Client sends Content-Type: text/plain on JSON body — model binding fails with 415.

blocks.text: OutputFormatterSelector scores formatters by media type match quality. [Produces] and format filters can short-circuit negotiation. System.Text.Json replaced Newtonsoft as default in ASP.NET Core 3.0 — AddNewtonsoftJson() still available for JsonProperty attributes and reference loop handling. Minimal APIs bypass full formatter pipeline for Results.Json but share HttpJsonOptions. For performance, source generators (JsonSerializable) reduce reflection. Production: fix JSON contract in OpenAPI; disable unused formatters to shrink attack surface; log 406 rates to detect client misconfiguration.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying content negotiation is 'always used' — most APIs are JSON-fixed. Not knowing System.Text.Json is default. Confusing Content-Type (request body format) with Accept (response preference). Unable to explain 406 vs 415.

interviewTakeaways: Output formatters serialize ObjectResult values; Accept header drives selection among registered IOutputFormatter implementations.
Modern Web APIs standardize on JSON — configure JsonOptions and HttpJsonOptions consistently for controllers and minimal APIs.
Use File() or dedicated export routes for CSV/binary instead of over-engineering negotiation unless clients require Accept-driven formats.

60s: Handler returns object → ObjectResult → formatter selector reads Accept → System.Text.Json writes body. JSON-only is normal. 406 when no match. Content-Type is for request body; Accept is for response.
Follow-up: when would you choose Newtonsoft.Json over System.Text.Json?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'ASP.NET always negotiates XML and JSON' gets you rejected — JSON is default; XML is opt-in.
Only configuring AddJsonOptions but not ConfigureHttpJsonOptions — minimal and controller APIs serialize differently.
Strong answer: 'Formatters plug into ObjectResult execution. JSON via System.Text.Json. Align options. JSON-only for new APIs. Custom formatters or File() for exports.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express res.json() sets Content-Type: application/json explicitly. ASP.NET formatters set Content-Type during ObjectResult execution. Express has no Accept-driven formatter pipeline — you branch manually.
NestJS @Exclude() and @Expose() control JSON shape like JsonIgnoreCondition. ASP.NET uses System.Text.Json attributes ([JsonIgnore], [JsonPropertyName]).
